title: What Should I Do After a Positive Pregnancy Test?
seoTitle: After a positive pregnancy test: next steps
description: Arrange maternity contact, review medicines without stopping them alone, confirm pregnancy vitamins, and know which pain or bleeding needs emergency care.
primaryQuestion: What should I do after a positive pregnancy test?
directAnswer: After a positive home test, contact a local obstetric or maternity service promptly to begin antenatal care planning. If you take regular medicines or live with a long-term condition, speak to a doctor soon. UK NHS guidance says not to stop prescribed medicine until you have talked with a GP or specialist. Confirm folic acid and other pregnancy vitamins with a clinician; detail sits in our folic acid before pregnancy guide. Note the first day of your last period if you know it. Severe pain, heavy bleeding or fainting needs emergency care now.

sections.heading: Arrange care and everyday health steps
paragraphs: UK NHS advice is to tell maternity services as soon as you know you are pregnant so care and information can start. In India, use your local obstetrician, hospital antenatal clinic or the clinician who already knows your history. Appointment timing and booking rules differ by city and facility, so treat NHS self-referral logistics as UK-specific.

NHS pages also list stopping smoking, avoiding alcohol, and taking recommended pregnancy vitamins such as folic acid. Our preconception planning guide covers the broader checklist if vaccines and chronic-condition reviews are still open; start what you can now rather than waiting for a perfect plan.
A home test detects pregnancy hormone in urine. It does not confirm where the pregnancy is growing or whether later bleeding will be harmless.

sections.heading: Medicines, conditions and what to bring
paragraphs: Write down all medicines you take, including pharmacy purchases, Ayurvedic or herbal preparations and vitamins. If you find you are pregnant, NHS guidance says to keep taking prescribed medicine until a doctor has reviewed it, because stopping suddenly may cause more harm than a planned switch.

If you live with diabetes, thyroid disease, hypertension, epilepsy, sickle cell disease, HIV or another long-term condition, ask early how monitoring should change. Carry period dates, previous pregnancy outcomes, allergy lists and any recent blood or scan reports you already hold.

Jot questions about diet, work, travel, exercise and mental health before the visit so they are not lost in the moment. Prenatal physiotherapy questions can wait for a dedicated physio pathway once obstetric booking is underway.

sections.heading: What the first pregnancy visit usually covers
paragraphs: Expect history-taking, blood pressure, basic examination planning, discussion of blood tests and screening that fit local practice, and an estimated due date based on your dates, later refined by ultrasound when arranged. Schedules for dating scans are set by your clinicians; copying a UK week-number chart onto an Indian clinic diary can create false deadlines.
Ask who to call for non-urgent worries between visits, and which symptoms should bypass that route. Keep contact numbers for your clinic and local emergency services saved offline.

sections.heading: Symptoms that need urgent or emergency care
paragraphs: RCOG patient information on ectopic pregnancy advises seeking medical help immediately if you have concerning symptoms and have had sex in recent months, even if you do not think you could be pregnant, and even before a home test is positive. NHS ectopic guidance likewise says to seek advice if you might be pregnant with symptom combinations, including without a positive test.

Call emergency services in India on 112, or go to hospital emergency care, for severe tummy pain, pain in the tip of the shoulder, heavy bleeding that soaks a pad soon after putting it on, fainting, or feeling very dizzy and pale. Do not wait for a scheduled scan slot or a routine consult reply.

Lighter spotting without severe pain still deserves prompt maternity or early-pregnancy advice, and our bleeding in early pregnancy guide explains triage in more depth. Collapse-level symptoms are an emergency now.

faqs.question: Do I need to repeat the home test before calling a clinic?
faqs.answer: One clear positive is enough to start arranging care. Repeating strips can add confusion if lines change with hydration or timing. If symptoms are urgent, seek emergency assessment without waiting for another drugstore test.

faqs.question: What if the pregnancy was unplanned?
faqs.answer: You still deserve confidential information about options and antenatal care. Contact a clinician you trust promptly, especially if you take regular medicines. Support services exist for uncertainty; secrecy should not delay safety advice.

sourcesChecked.title: What to do when you find out you're pregnant

sourcesChecked.limitations: UK NHS pathway; Indian antenatal booking routes differ

sourcesChecked.passage: Contact your GP or call NHS 111 if you have a combination of any of the above symptoms and you might be pregnant – even if you haven't had a positive pregnancy test.
